newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Clinton urges EU to bring east Europe in from cold.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges EU to bring east Europe in from cold.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday urged western Europe to embrace the emerging democracies and markets of the former Soviet bloc to further the cause of European security, stability and trade.

Attending a twice-yearly summit with European Union leaders in The Hague, U.S. President Bill Clinton said more private investment needed to be pumped into east Europe's ex-communist states to build on already substantial aid from the West.

Amid security unprecedented in the Netherlands, Clinton and a host of European leaders met to commemorate the plan proposed in 1947 by then Secretary of State George Marshall that is credited with kick-starting Europe's shattered post-war economy.
"This meeting between the United States and the European Union is a symbol of how we're fulfilling the real dream and promise of the Marshall Plan," Clinton told reporters.
"The Marshall Plan...was open to all of Europe but for half the continent the dream of recovery was denied," he told a palace lunch hosted by Dutch Queen Beatrix.

"Now at last all of Europe's nations are seeking the right for places at our transatlantic table," he aid, adding that western leaders were "trustees of history's rarest gift, a second chance to complete the job that Marshall...began."
Clinton, Dutch premier Wim Kok and European Commission President Jacques Santer stopped short of announcing a second Marshall Plan, but urged greater efforts at integration.

"We can't simply say to those countries (in eastern Europe) 'We want you to be free democracies, we want you to have economic reform and good luck'," said Clinton, adding that work needed to be done with individual former Soviet bloc countries to see what sort of fresh action was necessary.

Clinton, noting that a more prosperous and united Europe would be a stronger partner for the U.S., was non-committal on plans for European monetary union, saying only that European integration was good for all.
"We are not only not threatened by that, we are excited about it, he said.

But he said it would be inappropriate for him to comment on the mechanics of a single currency, aimed at rivalling the dollar on global financial markets. "The decision to do that and the mechanics (of it) are a matter for the Union," he said.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said Washington was keen to see the EU expand as rapidly and widely as possible.
In an article for the International Herald Tribune, Albright urged people to stop talking of the "Eastern bloc" as if the Soviet-dominated Warsaw Pact military alliance still existed.

"It is time we stopped looking at Europe through Rip Van Winkle eyes. It is time to agree that there will not be a truly complete trans-Atlantic partnership in security and trade, or a truly 'European' currency or foreign policy, until it encompasses Europe's new market democracies.

The day after Clinton signalled a new era in global relations with the signing in Paris of an historic pact linking Cold War enemies NATO and Russia, he flew into The Netherlands to join the Marshall Plan festivities.

Clinton, accompanied by his wife Hillary, brought tight security to The Hague but delighted onlookers with an impromptu 10-minute canalside walk-about on his way from the U.S.-EU talks to a palace lunch appointment with Dutch Queen Beatrix.
The president's trip was, however, shadowed by a U.S. Supreme Court decision on Tuesday to let a sexual harassment lawsuit brought against him by Paula Jones go ahead.
"I really have nothing to add to what (lawyer Robert Bennett) said. The Supreme Court has made its decision," Clinton told reporters in his first public comment on the ruling.

Clinton was due later to address representatives of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which groups the United States and Canada with European nations, as part of the Marshall Plan celebrations and will then unveil a statue of Marshall in the port city of Rotterdam.
Earlier Washington and the 15-member European Union agreed a package of trade issues, averting a trans-Atlantic meat war and freeing up trade in products worth $40 billion a year.
